messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

On a humid July evening in 2013, 66‑year‑old Arun Reddy, a South‑Eastern Asian roofer, was working on a high‑rise roof in the heart of Chicago when a sudden burst in the building’s chemical containment system released a thick, acrid plume of a toxic solvent. The vapor drifted down the stairwell, staining his shirt and filling his lungs with a numbing cold. In the moment, he felt the world collapse: the sky turned a sickly green, his heartbeat hammered, and the sound of the wind outside seemed to echo the hiss of his own panic. The shock of that night became a vivid memory, a film that he can replay whenever the darkness falls over his home or the antiseptic scent of a hospital lingers in a grocery store aisle. The memory of that night is the engine of Arun’s distress. Whenever he wakes to the blackness of his bedroom, the absence of light forces that night into view, and the vividness of the chemical plume returns with every breath he takes. He can feel the solvent on his skin, the heat that burned his back, and the helplessness that pressed against his chest. Those images are accompanied by a sudden surge of emotional intensity, sometimes without a clear visual cue—an “emotion without image” that shakes him out of sleep. The terror of that chemical exposure makes him think the world is dangerous, a belief that he has carried for years. He tells himself that the risk he felt then still lingers in every new situation, and that belief makes him hyper‑vigilant to any smell that reminds him of that night. Arun’s intense appraisal that the world is dangerous translates into a sense of threat that dominates his daily life. He cannot relax even when he is in the safety of his own living room; his concentration falters on routine tasks, and he has learned to avoid unfamiliar places because he can no longer assess their danger. The persistent threat keeps the memory alive: each time he senses a new danger, his mind automatically flips back to the night he was exposed, reinforcing the loop that binds memory to threat. The more he feels threatened, the more he feels he cannot rely on himself to cope, and that doubt feeds a sense of hopelessness about his future. The triggers that Arun experiences are both environmental and sensory. The darkness of night, the smell of antiseptic, and other familiar odors that once seemed harmless now serve as alarms. Whenever one of these cues surfaces, he reacts by suppressing thoughts of the event, a maladaptive strategy he has adopted to stay afloat. By trying hard not to think about the spill, he avoids confronting the memory but also strengthens the belief that he cannot rely on himself to process the trauma. This suppression, in turn, amplifies his sense of threat—he feels less in control, and the threat of danger grows even larger. The same suppression also fuels his past dwelling: he often finds himself revisiting the moment he was on that roof, thinking of how he was before the accident, and this rumination is triggered by the same dark and olfactory cues that first triggered his suppression. Arun’s negative appraisal that the world is dangerous also makes him wary of asserting himself. In meetings with supervisors or when negotiating payment with clients, he never disagrees, believing that any conflict could expose him to more danger. The avoidance of assertiveness is a strategy that, once adopted, reinforces his hopelessness: he feels trapped in a life where he cannot voice his needs, and this fuels a deeper sense that he cannot rely on his own agency. Moreover, because he sees himself as incapable, he begins to perceive even ordinary smells—like the faint scent of fresh paint at a construction site—as potential triggers that will reopen the traumatic scene, further entrenching the loop of threat and avoidance. Over the past year, these intertwined patterns have begun to take a toll on Arun’s work and his marriage. His focus on the roof’s seams slips more often, and his partner, Maya, has grown increasingly worried that he will collapse from a sudden flare of anxiety. The night before their daughter’s school play, Arun could not relax; he imagined the chemical plume again, felt the same wave of terror, and stayed up until dawn, staring at the ceiling, listening for the hiss of unseen danger. That night’s sleeplessness made him believe his future is bleak, and the fear of being unable to protect his family finally prompted him to seek help. Arun hopes therapy can untangle the cycle that ties his memories to his triggers, relieve the relentless threat that keeps him from relaxing, and give him the tools to regain confidence in himself so that he may stop feeling doomed and begin to see a horizon beyond the chemical‑laden night.
